questions.answerKey: Loss of apparent weight=42.0−25.5=16.5 N. Relative density=weight in air/loss in water=42.0/16.5=28/11≈2.55, dimensionless.
questions.markingGuide: Independent SomaSmart self-assessment guidance, not an official NECTA marking scheme. Award1 each for weight-loss principle, difference16.5N, relative-density ratio, numerical value≈2.55, and correct dimensionless interpretation. The measured source values are used without replacing them with a tabulated aluminium density.

supplementalLessons.title: Mechanics, fluids and energy: prerequisite revision
objectives: Review force, pressure, buoyancy, motion and machine definitions.
Use consistent equations and distinguish actual from apparent quantities.
Interpret a source question without changing its given numerical values.
paragraphs: Legacy FormTwo examinations revisit force, pressure, motion, machines and energy. This is a supplemental revision chapter for previously introduced skills, not a claim that these are newly prescribed current FormTwo subtopics. Use the original source wording and diagrams when practising genuine questions.

Pressure is force per area, P=F/A. For a fluid at rest, the gauge pressure at depthh isρgh, so depth, density and gravity matter. A submerged body experiences upthrust equal to the weight of displaced fluid. Apparent weight is actual weight minus upthrust; immersion does not remove the gravitational attraction on the body.

Newton’s third-law forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions but act on different bodies. For one body accelerating upward, the force equation is T−mg=ma; do not cancel an interaction pair as though both forces acted on the same body. In constant acceleration, choose equations that match the available variables or calculate area beneath a velocity–time graph.

Mechanical advantage is actual load divided by effort. Efficiency is mechanical advantage divided by velocity ratio, expressed as a fraction or percentage. If actual mechanical advantage is already given, multiplying it by efficiency again changes its meaning. Work done against gravity ismgh, and average useful lifting power is work divided by elapsed time.
examples: An object is acted on by2N over10m², so pressure=2/10=0.2Pa. If instead pressure0.2Pa and force2N are known, area=2/0.2=10m².
A45kg climber accelerating upward at5.5m/s² withg=10m/s² requires rope tensionT=45(10+5.5)=697.5N. A550N limit is exceeded; the prescribed motion cannot continue with an intact rope.
A200kg load lifted12m in10s gains200×10×12=24000J of gravitational potential energy. Useful average power is24000/10=2400W; input power would require additional efficiency information.

supplementalLessons.title: Measurement and thermal properties: prerequisite revision
objectives: Review SI units and small-dimension measurement.
Distinguish a thermal measurement from a simplified application claim.
paragraphs: This supplemental chapter supports measurement and elementary thermal material revisited in legacy FormTwo assessments. It does not replace a current official topic index. Preserve printed units and compare source figures with any transcribed values before solving.

A physical measurement combines a numerical value and a unit. Length has SI unit metre, mass kilogram, current ampere and thermodynamic temperature kelvin. Displacement is a length vector; momentum is mass times velocity and therefore has unit kilogram metre per second. A micrometer measures small external dimensions using a screw mechanism.

To find an irregular solid’s volume by overflow, start with water at the Eureka-can spout level and collect all water displaced when the object is fully immersed. Read the collected volume at eye level. The method assumes the solid does not dissolve, absorb substantial water or trap an unaccounted air bubble; the object volume equals the displaced water volume.

Temperature measures thermal state. A clinical thermometer is intended for body temperature. Surface tension generally decreases as the temperature of a given liquid rises, but claims about flavour also involve sensory and chemical factors. Treat a multiple-choice physics explanation within its stated alternatives rather than turning a simplified example into a universal biological rule.
examples: If a micrometer main scale is2.50mm and its thimble shows38 divisions at0.01mm each, the reading is2.50+0.38=2.88mm before any zero correction.

A measuring cylinder reads300mL before a stone is submerged and700mL afterwards. The stone’s volume is700−300=400mL=400cm³; reversing the initial/final labels does not describe the physical sequence correctly.
A body with mass2kg moving at3m/s has momentum6kgm/s. Its mass unit remainskg, whereas momentum requires the additional length-per-time factor.
